era: The Seeker Who Crossed the World
teaser: He left Persia to find one man. It took him decades, several religions, and a spell as someone's property.
quran_mention: The noblest of you before Allah is the most God-fearing — Quran 49:13

layers.title: Who He Was
layers.subtitle: A boy whose job was to keep a fire alight
layers.content:
Almost everything known about his early life comes from him. Ibn Ishaq recorded it as a long first-person account, and it is preserved in Ibn Hisham's Sirah — the fullest conversion story in the whole tradition, told by a man who lived long enough to be asked.

The reports place his origin in Persia, in the district of Isfahan. His father was a landowner of some substance and, by Salman's own telling, loved him to the point of keeping him close and confined. The family religion was Zoroastrian. Salman's assigned duty in it was practical rather than mystical: he tended the sacred fire and made sure it did not go out.

That is the starting position. A comfortable Persian household, an only son kept indoors, and a boy whose religious life consisted of maintaining a flame he had not chosen.

He would end his life as an Arab-speaking Muslim in Iraq, a freed slave with no tribe to claim him, correcting the second caliph on the difference between a king and a khalifa. Nothing in between was accidental. He went looking.
layers.source: Ibn Ishaq's report from Salman al-Farsi, in Ibn Hisham, as-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: Four teachers, each dying and handing him on
layers.content:
He was sent out on an errand, passed a Christian church, went in to watch, and did not come back the same. When he told his father, his father put him in chains.

He escaped with a caravan to ash-Sham and attached himself to a bishop there — who, it turned out, was hoarding the charity people brought him. Salman said so publicly after the man died. He then served his successor, whom he describes as genuinely righteous, and when that man was dying Salman asked him where to go next. He was sent on to a man at Mosul. Then to Nasibin. Then to Ammuriya in the land of Rum. Each teacher died. Each pointed him further.

The last had no one left to send him to. He told Salman the time of a prophet had come, sent with the religion of Ibrahim, who would emigrate to a land of date palms lying between two fields of black rock. Then he named three marks by which he could be recognised.

The details vary between transmissions, and the place-names are given differently in different versions. What does not vary is the shape: years of travel, four separate teachers, and a description carried in his head from Persia to Arabia.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 29:69 — «وَالَّذِينَ جَاهَدُوا فِينَا لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا» — 'And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our ways'
layers.source: Ibn Ishaq's long report from Salman, in Ibn Hisham, as-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: He tested the three marks before he said a word
layers.content:
He did not arrive the way anyone plans to arrive. The Arabs he travelled with sold him, and he came into Madinah as another man's property. Which means the land reached him before the man did — he saw the date palms and the black rock and knew he had been delivered to the right place by people who meant him harm.

The three marks were a test he could run without asking a single question. He brought food and presented it as sadaqa; the Prophet ﷺ told those with him to eat, and did not eat. He brought food again and presented it as a gift; the Prophet ﷺ ate. Then he looked for the seal of prophethood between the shoulders, and saw it. Salman's account has him weeping at that point.

His slavery kept him out of Badr and out of Uhud. He was not free to go. The Prophet ﷺ directed that he be bought out of servitude and the Companions contributed to the price; reports differ on the exact terms of the ransom.

It is also reported that the Prophet ﷺ said of him, 'Salman is one of us, the People of the House.' The report is widely repeated. Scholars discuss its chain, and it is given here as a report, with no grading attached.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 7:157 — «يَجِدُونَهُ مَكْتُوبًا عِندَهُمْ فِي التَّوْرَاةِ وَالْإِنجِيلِ» — 'whom they find written with them in the Tawrah and the Injil'
layers.hadith_ref: 'Salman is one of us, the People of the House' — a widely transmitted report; presented without grading
layers.source: Ibn Ishaq's report from Salman, in Ibn Hisham, as-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: The Persian who told Madinah how to survive a siege
layers.content:
In the fifth year after the Hijrah the confederate armies moved on Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ convened a council and held a long discussion with his military leaders. The proposal that was adopted came from Salman.

His words were plain and technical: 'Messenger of Allah, whenever a siege was laid to us in Persia, we would dig trenches to defend ourselves.' Al-Mubarakpuri calls it an unprecedented plan of action in Arabia. Nobody there had fought this way. Salman was the only man present who had grown up somewhere that had.

The orders went out at once. Forty yards of digging were allotted to each group of ten men. The Prophet ﷺ dug with them, and encouraged them, and kept them mindful of the reward. Sahl ibn Sa'd said: we were in the company of Allah's Messenger, and some would dig and we would carry away the dirt on our backs. The hunger during those days bordered on starvation.

Al-Bara narrated that a boulder would not break, and the Prophet ﷺ struck it three times, naming ash-Sham and its red palaces, then Persia and the white palace of Mada'in, then Yemen and the gates of San'a. Ibn Ishaq reported something similar from Salman himself.

A Persian slave-turned-freedman heard his own country promised while digging a ditch with his hands.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 33:22 — «وَلَمَّا رَأَى الْمُؤْمِنُونَ الْأَحْزَابَ قَالُوا هَٰذَا مَا وَعَدَنَا اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ» — 'And when the believers saw the Confederates they said, this is what Allah and His Messenger promised us'
layers.hadith_ref: The boulder and the three strikes — narrated by al-Bara ibn Azib, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar; Ibn Ishaq reported similar from Salman (Ibn Hisham)
layers.source: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (The Invasion of al-Ahzab); Ibn Ishaq in Ibn Hisham, as-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: He asked Abu Bakr for advice and gave Umar none he wanted
layers.content:
Two conversations, both recorded by Ibn Sa'd, show what he became.

The first: 'I visited my father Abu Bakr as-Siddiq in the illness from which he died. I said, Caliph of the Messenger of Allah, instruct me. I do not think you will give me any instruction after this day.' Note the word he uses — my father. A Persian with no lineage in Arabia, claiming a man by affection. Abu Bakr's answer was about the conquests that were coming: I do not know what your portion will be of what you put in your stomach or throw on your back. Know that Allah is responsible for whoever prays the five prayers. And do not kill anyone under the protection of Allah.

The second is shorter and harder. Umar ibn al-Khattab asked him: are we a kingdom or a caliphate? Salman answered, 'If you collect from the land of the Muslims a dirham, or more, or less, and then spend it wrongfully, you are a king and not a caliph.' Ibn Sa'd's next sentence is three words long. Umar wept.

The man who had been sold on a roadside told the ruler of two fallen empires the condition on which his authority was legitimate, and was neither punished nor thanked — he was believed.

Reports on the year of his death and his age differ so widely that the biographers flag the disagreement rather than settle it. May Allah be pleased with him. He walked out of Isfahan to find one man, and he found him.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 49:13 — «إِنَّ أَكْرَمَكُمْ عِندَ اللَّهِ أَتْقَاكُمْ» — 'Indeed the noblest of you in the sight of Allah is the most God-fearing of you'
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley (Usayr via Abu Imran al-Jawni; Zadan via Ata ibn as-Sa'ib)

quiz.prompt: What was Salman's religious duty in his father's household in Persia?

options.text: Copying scriptures
Tending the sacred fire and keeping it from going out
Serving as a temple guard
Collecting offerings from tenants

quiz.citation: Ibn Ishaq's report from Salman, in Ibn Hisham, as-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah
quiz.scholar_reflection: It was a maintenance job, not a calling. He was responsible for a flame he had inherited, which may be why a religion he had to reason his way into meant so much to him.

quiz.prompt: How did his search proceed after he left Persia?

options.text: He travelled alone with no guidance
He served a succession of Christian teachers, each of whom died and directed him to the next
He studied in a single monastery for twenty years
He was taught by Jewish scholars in Yathrib

quiz.citation: Ibn Ishaq's long report from Salman, in Ibn Hisham, as-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah
quiz.scholar_reflection: The first he served turned out to be hoarding the people's charity, and Salman exposed him. The rest he describes as righteous men. Each one handed him on before dying, until the last had no one left to send him to.

quiz.prompt: How did Salman arrive in Madinah?

options.text: As an invited guest of the Ansar
As a merchant with his own caravan
As a slave, having been sold by the Arabs he travelled with
As an envoy from the Byzantine frontier

quiz.citation: Ibn Ishaq's report from Salman, in Ibn Hisham, as-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah
quiz.scholar_reflection: He recognised the place before he met the man — the date palms between two fields of black rock, exactly as described to him. He had been delivered to the right city by people who were betraying him.

quiz.prompt: What did Salman propose at the council before the Battle of the Trench?

options.text: That the Muslims meet the Confederates in open battle
That Madinah be evacuated
That a trench be dug as a defensive perimeter around the city
That a treaty be sought with Ghatafan

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (The Invasion of al-Ahzab)
quiz.scholar_reflection: His reasoning was experience, not theory: whenever a siege was laid to us in Persia, we would dig trenches to defend ourselves. Al-Mubarakpuri notes it was unprecedented in Arabia. The Prophet ﷺ adopted it and dug alongside everyone else.

quiz.prompt: What did Salman say when Umar asked him whether they were a kingdom or a caliphate?

options.text: That the question was not his to answer
That taking a dirham from the Muslims' land and spending it wrongfully makes you a king, not a caliph
That the caliphate had already ended
That only the conquests would decide it

quiz.citation: Reported from Zadan through Ata ibn as-Sa'ib, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ibn Sa'd records the response in two words: Umar wept. He had asked a question he already feared the answer to, and he asked it of the one man with no clan interest in flattering him.

quiz.prompt: Salman spent years and several countries looking for something he could not name precisely. Have you ever searched like that?

options.text: Yes, and I am still in the middle of it
I inherited my faith and never had to search
I searched, found it, and now have to keep choosing it
I am not sure I would recognise the answer if I found it

quiz.citation: Reflection on Ibn Ishaq's report from Salman, in Ibn Hisham
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had no map and no timeline. What he had was a willingness to keep moving when each teacher died, and a description he refused to forget.

quiz.prompt: His father chained him to keep him from leaving. Where does love of family sit against following what you believe is true?

options.text: It is the hardest tension in my life
My family and my faith point the same way, and I know that is rare
I have compromised to keep the peace and I am not proud of it
I left, and I carry the cost of it

quiz.citation: Reflection on Salman's account of leaving his father's house, in Ibn Hisham
quiz.scholar_reflection: The report does not present his father as cruel. It presents him as a man who loved his son and could not let him go, which is the more difficult version of the story.

quiz.prompt: He brought experience from a completely different world and it saved Madinah. What do you carry from where you came from that your community does not have?

options.text: A skill nobody here has thought to ask for
A way of seeing things that gets me labelled difficult
Nothing I have identified — I mostly try to fit in
The perspective of someone who arrived rather than was born here

quiz.citation: Reflection on al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (The Invasion of al-Ahzab)
quiz.scholar_reflection: In a council of Arab military leaders discussing an Arabian problem, the decisive contribution came from the man who had grown up somewhere else entirely. He offered it as a fact about Persia, not a claim about himself.

quiz.prompt: He tested the three marks quietly before saying anything. Is careful verification a strength or a hesitation?

options.text: A strength. Conviction should be checkable.
I use it as an excuse to delay committing
I tend to leap and then look for reasons
Depends whether I want the answer to be yes

quiz.citation: Reflection on Salman's account of the three signs, in Ibn Hisham
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had crossed continents on the strength of that description. He still ran the tests. Wanting something to be true did not stop him checking whether it was.

quiz.prompt: He told the most powerful man alive the exact condition on which his authority was legitimate. Who can say that to you, and who can you say it to?

options.text: Nobody, in either direction, and that is a problem
One person, and I protect that relationship
I can hear it more easily than I can say it
I say it and it costs me every time

quiz.citation: Reported from Zadan, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Umar sought him out to ask. That is the part usually skipped: the correction was invited. A ruler who arranges to be told the truth has done most of the work already.
